Homeostasis.intro: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment. It ensures cells can function correctly despite changes in conditions.
Homeostasis.mnemonic: Think of homeostasis as the body's 'THERMOSTAT': Temperature, Hormones, Electrolytes, Respiration, Metabolism, Osmosis, Sugar, Toxins, and Acidity are all regulated. Or remember the feedback loop: 'RRCEF' — Receptor detects change, Response triggered, Corrects the error, Effectors act, Feedback returns to normal.

sections.title: What is Homeostasis?
sections.text: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment of the body stable so that cells can function optimally.
points: Internal conditions regulated — body temperature (37°C), blood glucose concentration, water content of the blood
Negative feedback — when conditions deviate from the set point, the response corrects them back
Set point — the ideal value the body aims to maintain (e.g. 37°C for body temperature)
Automatic control — homeostatic responses do not require conscious thought
Why it matters — enzymes work at an optimal temperature and pH; cells need stable water potential to function

sections.title: Negative Feedback
sections.text: Negative feedback is the mechanism that brings any deviation back toward the set point.
points: Receptor — detects the stimulus and sends information to the control centre
Control centre — processes the information and coordinates the response (e.g. hypothalamus for temperature)
Effector — a muscle or gland that carries out the corrective response
Opposes the change — if temperature rises, response cools the body; if it falls, response warms it

callout.label: Key Concept
callout.text: Negative feedback always returns conditions BACK to the normal level. Response always OPPOSES the original change.

sections.title: Temperature Regulation
sections.text: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat, detecting blood temperature and coordinating responses.
points: Too hot — sweat glands produce sweat (evaporation cools skin); vasodilation (blood vessels near skin widen, more heat lost by radiation)
Too cold — vasoconstriction (blood vessels near skin narrow, less heat lost); shivering (muscle contractions generate heat); hairs stand on end (traps air insulation layer)
Hypothalamus — the thermoregulatory centre in the brain that detects and controls temperature
Core temperature — the temperature deep within the body, kept at approximately 37°C

keyTerms.def: Maintenance of a stable internal environment
A control mechanism where the response reverses the original change
A muscle or gland that brings about a response
A cell or organ that detects a change (stimulus) in the environment
The ideal value that homeostatic mechanisms aim to maintain
Widening of blood vessels near the skin to increase heat loss
Narrowing of blood vessels near the skin to reduce heat loss
The region of the brain that acts as the body's thermostat

examTips: Negative feedback always returns to the set point — the response opposes the change, never amplifies it.
Name all three conditions regulated: body temperature, blood glucose concentration, and water content.
For temperature questions, distinguish between vasodilation (widening) and vasoconstriction (narrowing) — and know which direction each causes heat loss to change.
commonMistakes: Confusing negative feedback (corrects and returns to set point) with positive feedback (amplifies the change further — e.g. childbirth contractions).
Saying blood vessels 'move closer to' or 'away from' the skin — the vessels don't move. They widen (vasodilation) or narrow (vasoconstriction) in place.
Forgetting that shivering generates heat through rapid muscle contractions — it is an effector response, not just a sensation.
clozePassages: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes in external conditions. The body regulates blood glucose concentration, body temperature, and water content. These are controlled by negative feedback mechanisms — when a condition moves away from its set point, receptors detect this and effectors bring it back. Examples include sweating to cool down and shivering to warm up.

Negative feedback is the mechanism used in homeostasis to keep conditions within a narrow range. When a variable deviates from its set point, receptors detect the change and send signals to a control centre. The control centre sends instructions to effectors such as muscles or glands to counteract the change. This brings the variable back to the set point, completing the feedback loop.

The body regulates temperature through several mechanisms. When too hot, sweat glands produce sweat which cools the skin as it evaporates. Vasodilation occurs — blood vessels near the skin surface widen, allowing more heat to radiate away. When too cold, vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin. Shivering occurs — rapid muscle contractions generate heat. All these responses are controlled by the hypothalamus.

Nervous System.intro: The nervous system allows rapid detection and response to changes. It consists of the CNS (brain and spinal cord) and peripheral nerves.
Nervous System.mnemonic: Remember the reflex arc order with: 'Silly Rabbits Should Run More' — Stimulus, Receptor, Sensory neurone, Relay neurone, Motor neurone (then effector). For neurone direction: 'Sensory = Sends TO brain; Motor = Moves FROM brain'.

sections.title: Structure of the Nervous System
sections.text: The nervous system is divided into the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system.
points: CNS — brain and spinal cord; the control centre for the whole body
Sensory neurones — carry impulses FROM receptors TO the CNS
Motor neurones — carry impulses FROM the CNS TO effectors
Relay neurones — connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS
Effectors — muscles (contract) or glands (secrete) that produce the response

sections.title: Reflex Arc
sections.text: A reflex is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious decision-making.
points: Speed — reflexes bypass the brain, so the response is faster than voluntary actions
Automatic — no conscious thought required; happens without decision-making
Examples — knee-jerk reflex, pupil reflex, withdrawal of hand from heat
Protective function — reflexes often protect the body from harm

callout.label: Why Reflexes Are Fast
callout.text: Reflexes bypass the brain — coordinated in spinal cord. Pupil reflex, withdrawal reflex.

sections.title: Synapses
sections.text: Synapses are junctions between neurones where chemical signals transfer the electrical message.
points: Synapse — the tiny gap between the end of one neurone and the start of the next
Neurotransmitters — chemical molecules released into the synaptic gap to carry the signal
Diffusion — neurotransmitters diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors on the next neurone
New impulse — binding triggers a new electrical impulse in the next neurone
Drugs — many drugs affect synaptic transmission by blocking receptors or preventing reuptake of neurotransmitters

keyTerms.def: Nerve cell carrying electrical impulses
Gap between neurones — neurotransmitters carry signal across
Pathway of neurones in a reflex action
Central nervous system — brain and spinal cord
Chemical released at a synapse that carries the signal to the next neurone
A cell that detects a stimulus and converts it to an electrical impulse
Neurone carrying impulses from receptors to the CNS
Neurone carrying impulses from the CNS to effectors

examTips: Reflexes bypass the brain — they are coordinated in the spinal cord, which is why they are faster than voluntary responses.
Sensory neurones carry impulses TO the CNS; Motor neurones carry impulses FROM the CNS — remember: Sensory = inward, Motor = outward.
At synapses, electrical impulses are converted to chemical signals (neurotransmitters) — make sure you describe this two-step process in exam answers.
commonMistakes: Saying reflexes involve conscious thought — they do not. The brain may become aware of the reflex AFTER it happens, but it does not initiate it.
Confusing sensory and motor neurones — remember 'Sensory = TO brain, Motor = FROM brain'.
Describing synapses as electrical connections — they are chemical junctions; neurotransmitters diffuse across the gap.
clozePassages: The nervous system detects and responds to changes in the environment. Receptors in sense organs detect stimuli. Electrical impulses travel along sensory neurones to the brain or spinal cord. The brain processes the information and sends impulses along motor neurones to effectors such as muscles or glands, which produce a response. This pathway is called a stimulus-response pathway.

A reflex arc is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought. The pathway goes: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in spinal cord → motor neurone → effector → response. Reflexes are faster than voluntary responses because they bypass the brain. Examples include the knee-jerk reflex and withdrawing your hand from a hot object.

Synapses are junctions between neurones. When an electrical impulse reaches a synapse, neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic gap. These chemicals diffuse across and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. Drugs and toxins can affect synaptic transmission — for example, some drugs block neurotransmitter receptors or prevent their reuptake.

Hormones.intro: Hormones are chemical messengers produced by glands, carried in blood to target organs. Slower and longer-lasting than nervous responses.
Hormones.mnemonic: To remember key hormones and their glands, use: 'Adrenal glands = Adrenaline (fight/flight); Pancreas = Insulin/glucagon (glucose); Ovaries = Oestrogen; Testes = Testosterone; Pituitary = FSH/LH'. Nervous vs Hormonal: FEELS — Fast Electrical Exact Local Short-lived (nervous) vs SCABS — Slow Chemical All-body Blood-carried Sustained (hormonal).

sections.title: Nervous vs Hormonal
sections.text: The nervous and hormonal systems both coordinate responses but work in very different ways.
points: Nervous system — fast, short-lived, electrical impulse, travels along specific neurones to specific muscles/glands
Hormonal system — slower, longer-lasting, chemical messenger, carried in blood to all parts of body
Target organ specificity — hormones travel everywhere in blood but only affect cells with the right receptors
Combined action — some responses involve both systems working together (e.g. adrenaline and the nervous system in a fight-or-flight response)

sections.title: Key Hormones
sections.text: You need to know the main hormones, where they are produced, and what they do.
points: Adrenaline — adrenal glands; fight or flight response; increases heart rate, dilates pupils, redirects blood to muscles
Insulin — pancreas (beta cells); lowers blood glucose by stimulating uptake and glycogen storage
Glucagon — pancreas (alpha cells); raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown
Oestrogen — ovaries; controls female puberty and the menstrual cycle; triggers LH surge
Testosterone — testes; controls male puberty, sperm production, secondary sexual characteristics
FSH and LH — pituitary gland; control the menstrual cycle and egg/sperm development

sections.title: The Endocrine System
sections.text: The endocrine system is a collection of glands that produce and secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
points: Pituitary gland — the 'master gland'; produces FSH, LH, ADH and other hormones that control other glands
Thyroid gland — produces thyroxine, which controls metabolic rate
Adrenal glands — produce adrenaline for emergency responses
Pancreas — produces insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose
Ovaries/testes — produce sex hormones controlling reproduction and puberty

keyTerms.def: Chemical messenger carried in blood to target organs
Fight or flight hormone from adrenal glands
Organ that responds to a specific hormone
A gland that secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream
The master gland in the brain that controls other endocrine glands
Male sex hormone produced by the testes; controls puberty and sperm production
Female sex hormone produced by ovaries; controls puberty and menstrual cycle

examTips: Hormones travel in blood — they reach ALL organs but only affect target organs that have the correct receptors.
Hormonal responses are slow and long-lasting; Nervous responses are fast and short-lived — always compare both features in contrast questions.
Know at least five endocrine glands, the hormone each produces, and the effect — pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, ovaries/testes.
commonMistakes: Saying hormones travel through nerves — they travel in the bloodstream, not along nerves.
Confusing the speed: hormonal responses are SLOW (minutes to hours); nervous responses are FAST (milliseconds).
Forgetting that the pituitary gland is the 'master gland' — it controls many other endocrine glands.
clozePassages: Hormones are chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands and released into the bloodstream. They travel to target organs where they produce a response. Hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting than nervous responses. Key endocrine glands include the pituitary gland (the master gland), thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas, and reproductive organs.

The menstrual cycle is controlled by several hormones. FSH (follicle stimulating hormone) from the pituitary gland stimulates an egg to develop. Oestrogen from the ovaries causes the uterus lining to thicken. LH (luteinising hormone) triggers ovulation. Progesterone maintains the uterine lining after ovulation. If fertilisation does not occur, hormone levels fall and menstruation begins.

Hormonal contraception works by preventing ovulation or fertilisation. The contraceptive pill contains oestrogen and progesterone which inhibit FSH production, preventing eggs from maturing. Progesterone-only pills thicken cervical mucus to prevent sperm entry. IUDs prevent implantation of fertilised eggs. Hormonal contraceptives are highly effective but do not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

Blood Glucose.intro: Blood glucose must be kept within a narrow range. Insulin and glucagon work together as a negative feedback pair to achieve this.
Blood Glucose.mnemonic: Remember with 'I Go Down, Glucagon Goes Up': Insulin is released when glucose is high (brings it Down); Glucagon is released when glucose is low (brings it Up). Or picture a seesaw — when glucose is high, insulin tips the seesaw down; when glucose is low, glucagon tips it back up. Never confuse glycoGEN (storage) with glucaGON (the hormone that mobilises it).

sections.title: Blood Glucose Regulation
sections.text: The pancreas monitors blood glucose continuously and releases hormones to correct any deviation.
points: High glucose — pancreas releases INSULIN → cells take up glucose → liver converts glucose to glycogen → blood glucose falls
Low glucose — pancreas releases GLUCAGON → liver converts glycogen back to glucose → glucose released into blood → glucose rises
Negative feedback — insulin and glucagon are antagonistic hormones working as a pair
Glycogen — the storage polysaccharide in the liver and muscles; made from glucose and broken back down as needed
Target organs — liver cells and body cells respond to insulin; liver responds to glucagon

callout.label: Negative Feedback Pair
callout.text: Insulin lowers glucose. Glucagon raises glucose. They are antagonistic hormones.

sections.title: Diabetes
sections.text: Diabetes is a condition where blood glucose is not controlled properly.
points: Type 1 diabetes — autoimmune condition; pancreas produces no insulin; blood glucose cannot be lowered; requires daily insulin injections
Type 2 diabetes — cells become less responsive to insulin (insulin resistance); linked to obesity and poor diet; managed by diet, exercise, and medication
Symptoms — high blood glucose causes thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and blurred vision
Complications — uncontrolled diabetes damages blood vessels and nerves over time
Treatment differences — Type 1 always needs insulin; Type 2 may be managed without insulin initially

sections.title: Insulin and the Body
sections.text: Understanding how insulin works at the cellular level helps explain both normal regulation and diabetes.
points: Insulin receptors — found on body cells; insulin binds to these to allow glucose uptake
Glucose uptake — insulin increases the rate at which cells absorb glucose from the blood
Glycogenesis — conversion of glucose to glycogen in the liver (stimulated by insulin)
Glycogenolysis — breakdown of glycogen to glucose (stimulated by glucagon)
Insulin therapy — Type 1 diabetics inject insulin to replace what the pancreas cannot produce; doses timed with meals

keyTerms.def: Lowers blood glucose — stimulates glycogen storage
Raises blood glucose — stimulates glycogen breakdown
Storage form of glucose in liver and muscles
Pancreas produces no insulin — requires injections
Cells resistant to insulin — linked to lifestyle
Organ that produces both insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose
Conversion of glucose into glycogen for storage
Breakdown of glycogen back into glucose, stimulated by glucagon

examTips: Insulin = stores glucose as glycogen (glucose goes IN to storage). Glucagon = releases glucose from glycogen (glucose comes OUT of storage).
Glycogen and glucagon sound similar but are completely different — glycogen is the storage molecule; glucagon is the hormone that breaks it down.
Type 1 is always treated with insulin injections because no insulin is produced. Type 2 is often managed initially with lifestyle changes — this distinction is commonly tested.
commonMistakes: Mixing up insulin and glucagon — insulin LOWERS blood glucose; glucagon RAISES it.
Forgetting that glycogen is stored in BOTH the liver AND muscles — not just the liver.
Saying Type 2 diabetes means the pancreas stops working — it still produces insulin, but the cells no longer respond to it properly.
clozePassages: Blood glucose concentration is regulated by the pancreas. After a meal, blood glucose rises. The pancreas releases insulin, which causes cells to take up glucose from the blood. Excess glucose is converted to glycogen and stored in the liver and muscles. When blood glucose falls too low, the pancreas releases glucagon, which stimulates the liver to convert glycogen back to glucose.

Type 1 diabetes is caused by the immune system destroying the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. Sufferers must inject insulin daily to regulate blood glucose. Type 2 diabetes occurs when cells become less responsive to insulin. It is linked to obesity and can often be managed through diet and exercise. Without treatment, high blood glucose causes damage to blood vessels and nerves.

Glucagon and insulin work antagonistically to regulate blood glucose levels — this is an example of negative feedback. When glucose is too high, insulin is released and glucose is removed from the blood. When glucose is too low, glucagon is released and glucose is added to the blood. This keeps blood glucose within a narrow range, ensuring cells always have enough glucose for respiration.

Reproduction.intro: Reproduction is controlled by hormones. The menstrual cycle involves four key hormones, and fertility can be controlled using synthetic hormones.
Reproduction.mnemonic: Remember the four menstrual cycle hormones in order with: 'For Ovulation, Look Prepared' — FSH, Oestrogen, LH, Progesterone. For what each does: FSH = Follicle stimulated (egg matures); Oestrogen = lining builds and LH triggered; LH = launches egg (ovulation day 14); Progesterone = Protects lining (maintains uterus).

sections.title: The Menstrual Cycle
sections.text: The menstrual cycle is a monthly cycle of hormonal changes that prepares the body for potential pregnancy.
points: FSH (pituitary gland) — stimulates follicle and egg maturation; stimulates oestrogen production
Oestrogen (ovary) — repairs and thickens the uterus lining; inhibits FSH (negative feedback); stimulates LH surge
LH (pituitary gland) — triggers ovulation at approximately day 14
Progesterone (corpus luteum) — maintains the uterus lining; inhibits FSH and LH; falls at end of cycle triggering menstruation
Negative feedback — oestrogen inhibits FSH; progesterone inhibits FSH and LH

sections.title: Contraception
sections.text: Contraception prevents pregnancy by interfering with fertilisation, ovulation, or implantation.
points: Combined pill — contains oestrogen and progesterone; inhibits FSH production; prevents egg maturation and ovulation
Progesterone-only pill — thickens cervical mucus; prevents sperm reaching egg
Implant/injection — long-acting progesterone hormone; same mechanism as progesterone pill
Barrier methods — condoms, diaphragm; physically prevent sperm reaching egg; not hormonal; also protect against STIs
IUD — intrauterine device; prevents implantation; some release hormones

sections.title: IVF
sections.text: In vitro fertilisation (IVF) is a fertility treatment where fertilisation takes place outside the body.
points: Step 1 — FSH and LH given to stimulate multiple egg production
Step 2 — eggs collected surgically and fertilised with sperm outside the body
Step 3 — embryo(s) checked and one or two implanted into the uterus
Success rate — relatively low (around 25-30% per cycle); decreases with age
Ethical issues — unused embryos are destroyed; risk of multiple pregnancies; emotional and physical strain on the mother

keyTerms.def: Follicle-stimulating hormone — stimulates egg maturation
Luteinising hormone — triggers ovulation
Rebuilds uterus lining; triggers LH surge
Maintains uterus lining after ovulation
In vitro fertilisation — fertilisation outside the body
Release of a mature egg from the ovary (approximately day 14)
Structure that forms after ovulation and produces progesterone
Methods used to prevent pregnancy

examTips: FSH stimulates oestrogen production; oestrogen then inhibits FSH — this is negative feedback within the menstrual cycle.
IVF uses FSH and LH to stimulate multiple egg production so that several eggs can be collected in one cycle.
For evaluate questions on IVF, give both sides: benefits (helps infertile couples have children) and drawbacks (low success rate, ethical issues with unused embryos, risk of multiple births).
commonMistakes: Confusing FSH (stimulates egg maturation in the follicle) with LH (triggers the actual release of the egg at ovulation — day 14).
Forgetting that oestrogen INHIBITS FSH — this negative feedback prevents multiple eggs maturing at once.
Saying the pill prevents fertilisation — the combined pill primarily prevents ovulation (no egg = no fertilisation possible), not fertilisation itself.
clozePassages: Puberty is triggered by the release of sex hormones. In males, testosterone from the testes stimulates sperm production and the development of secondary sexual characteristics. In females, oestrogen from the ovaries stimulates egg maturation and secondary sexual characteristics. Puberty in females also involves the beginning of the menstrual cycle. The pituitary gland controls the release of these sex hormones.

IVF (in vitro fertilisation) is a fertility treatment used when natural conception is not possible. The woman is given FSH and LH to stimulate multiple eggs to mature. Eggs are collected and fertilised with sperm outside the body. The resulting embryos are checked for genetic disorders if required, then one or two are placed in the uterus. IVF has a relatively low success rate and raises ethical questions about unused embryos.

Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of a male gamete (sperm) and female gamete (egg) at fertilisation. The resulting zygote has a unique combination of genetic material from both parents, producing variation. Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and produces genetically identical offspring called clones. Plants such as strawberries reproduce asexually by sending out runners. Asexual reproduction is faster but produces no genetic variation.
